t: Korea. Nineteen fifty-one. A warship's surgeon pulls a bullet out of a soldier's chest.
Sixteen wounded men. Sixteen operations. Not one of them dies.
There's just one problem. He's not a surgeon.
He has never been to medical school. A few months ago, he was a monk.
His name is Fred Demara. And he has been a lot of people.
Lawrence, Massachusetts. Fred's father runs the film projectors in the city's theaters.
The family lives well. Then the Great Depression takes almost everything.
At sixteen, Fred runs away from home. To become a monk.
After two years, the monks tell him he's not suited for it.
So he joins the army. That doesn't suit him either.
In nineteen forty-two, he borrows an army buddy's name, Anthony Ignolia. And walks away.
He tries two more monasteries. Then he joins the navy.
There, he trains as a hospital corpsman. A medic's helper. Remember that.
The navy won't give him the job he wants.
So Fred fakes his own suicide.
And comes back as Doctor Robert Linton French. Psychologist.
Good morning, class. Today, we study the human mind.
Doctor French teaches psychology at a college in Pennsylvania.
He becomes the dean of its School of Philosophy.
He even publishes a booklet. How to Bring Up Your Child.
Then come a few forged checks. And Doctor French is gone.
The FBI finally catches up with him.
Eighteen months in a navy prison. For desertion.
Most people would take the hint.
Fred studies law at night. Under a fake name, of course.
Then he joins a Catholic teaching order in Maine. As Brother John Payne.
Brother John decides the order needs a college. So he founds one.
A real college. The state of Maine gives it a charter.
Then the order doesn't make him its head. So Brother John quits.
The college survives without him. Today, it's a university in Ohio.
But before he leaves Maine, Brother John makes a new friend.
A young doctor named Joseph Cyr.
Doctor, could I borrow your papers? I'm thinking of studying medicine.
Of course, Brother. Anything to help.
Fred studies those papers very closely. Then he disappears with them.
March, nineteen fifty-one. Saint John, New Brunswick. A navy recruiting office.
Doctor Joseph Cyr. I'd like to serve my country.
A doctor? Sir, we need doctors badly.
If the navy can't use me, I'm sure the army can. Or the air force.
Canada is fighting in Korea. Every service is short of doctors.
Normally, joining up takes about two months.
Nobody checks his papers.
The navy is so happy, nobody asks a single question.
Three days later, Fred is Surgeon-Lieutenant Joseph Cyr. Royal Canadian Navy.
His first posting is the naval hospital near Halifax.
His method is simple. Lots of penicillin. And lots of asking other doctors.
Colleagues remember a pleasant man. Fairly competent. Not much of a party guy.
He doesn't approve of how much the other officers drink.
Then, in June, the real test.
June fifteenth. Esquimalt, British Columbia.
Fred joins the destroyer H M C S Cayuga. Two hundred men, and one doctor.
Three days later, the Cayuga sails for Korea.
At sea, the work is easy. Cuts, sprains, the odd broken bone.
When a case is new, Doctor Cyr excuses himself. And reads up in his cabin.
Then the captain gets a toothache.
Doctor, this tooth is killing me.
One moment, Captain. I need to... prepare.
Fred has never pulled a tooth in his life.
He goes to his cabin. Opens a book. Reads.
Then he comes back, and pulls the tooth. No fuss.
Best tooth-pulling I've ever had.
Off the coast of Korea, the Cayuga supports a commando raid.
A boat comes alongside, full of wounded Korean soldiers.
Sixteen of them. Some will die without surgery.
Doc! They're bringing them aboard!
Every eye on the ship turns to the only surgeon on board.
Doc, are you ready?
Almost. Just... checking something.
Get them into the operating room. Prep them. I'll be right there.
Then he goes to his cabin. With a textbook on general surgery.
And he speed-reads it.
He comes out. Scrubs in. And starts cutting.
Major chest surgery. A bullet, deep in a man's chest.
He takes it out.
When it's over, none of the sixteen has died on his table.
Years later, some sailors would say it didn't happen quite like that. But the legend sticks.
Our doctor's a hero!
The ship's press officer loves this story. He writes it up.
Soon, newspapers all over Canada are running it.
Which is a problem. Because one of those papers lands in Grand Falls, New Brunswick.
Where Doctor Joseph Cyr is seeing patients. The real one.
Doctor Cyr is startled to read about his own adventures at sea.
That's my name. But I've never been to Korea.
October. A signal reaches the Cayuga. Your doctor is an impostor.
The captain can't believe it. His doctor is capable. And popular.
The crew doesn't believe it either. They go to his cabin.
Doc... tell us it isn't true.
Impossible. The man fixed my tooth.
The next day, a second signal. No doubt left.
Fred locks himself in his cabin. Then he gives up.
He's sent home on a British cruiser, by way of Japan.
Back in Canada, the navy holds an inquiry.
No charges. An honorable release.
And several hundred dollars in back pay.
The navy fires him. And pays him for his time.
He goes back to the States. A little richer. And very famous.
Fred sells his story to Life magazine.
It runs in January, nineteen fifty-two.
Which is great for money. And terrible for a man who changes names.
With fake papers, he gets a prison job in Huntsville, Texas.
Everything goes fine. Until an inmate finds an old copy of Life.
Hey, boss. Ain't this you?
Caught by his own story. Again.
By now, Fred is a big man. Hard to miss. Bad news for a master of disguise.
In nineteen fifty-nine, he even goes on Groucho Marx's quiz show. He wins a thousand dollars.
He says it's going to the Feed and Clothe Fred Demara Fund.
A bestselling book follows: The Great Impostor. Then Hollywood makes a movie.
Tony Curtis plays Fred.
Fred himself gets a small part in another film. As a hospital surgeon.
The man who fooled a whole navy... can't fool a camera. He's a terrible actor.
He becomes a counselor at a rescue mission in Los Angeles.
He even earns a certificate in Bible studies. A real one, this time.
In his last years, Fred works as a hospital chaplain in California.
His past comes out. The chief of staff stands up for him. He stays.
Fred Demara dies in nineteen eighty-two. He's sixty.
Monk. Psychologist. Dean. Surgeon. Prison officer. Chaplain.
In nineteen eighty, he sits beside a dying Hollywood star. Steve McQueen.
But that's another story.
